demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about why the event has happened to me
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

issues.item: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items imply an ongoing external danger/escape-monitoring profile more typical of fear-based threat from assault, accident re-exposure, or unsafe environments. That does not fit well with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another,' where the central disturbance is more plausibly guilt, responsibility, and intrusive memory rather than escape positioning.

Mirror checking is not clinically coherent with the rest of this profile. For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another, the other selected items center on dissociative/fragmented memory and guilt-focused rumination/meaning seeking. Mirror checking instead suggests appearance/body/reality checking behavior that is not supported by the memory items, not linked by the formulation's active edges, and is hard to explain as part of the same PTSD presentation here.

vignette: Manaia had always taken pride in her work as a security guard at a busy downtown office building. She was diligent and alert, with a keen eye for detail. But on that fateful evening two years ago, something went terribly wrong. As she was patrolling the lobby, she accidentally triggered a false alarm, which led to a chaotic evacuation of the building. In the ensuing chaos, an elderly man tripped on the stairs and fell, suffering a serious head injury. The event replayed in Manaia's mind like a broken record, with some parts eerily vivid and others frustratingly hazy. She remembered the sound of shattering glass, the sight of the man's crumpled body, and the feeling of her heart racing as she rushed to his side. But there were also gaping holes in her memory - moments she couldn't recall no matter how hard she tried. The more she thought about it, the more it felt like someone else's memory, not hers. As the days turned into weeks, Manaia found herself consumed by self-blame and rumination. Why had she been so careless? What if she hadn't triggered that alarm? She would lie awake at night, replaying every detail of the event, searching for answers to questions that seemed to have no resolution. Her friends and family tried to reassure her that it was an accident, but Manaia couldn't shake off the feeling that she was responsible. The memories haunted her, but they also felt strangely detached - as if she was recalling a scene from a movie rather than a real event. Sometimes, when she thought about that night, she felt nothing at all - no sadness, no guilt, just numbness. It was as if she had been observing herself from outside her body, watching the events unfold with a sense of disconnection. Manaia's obsession with understanding what had happened took over her life. She spent hours researching security protocols, pouring over incident reports, and even consulting with experts in the field. Her shifts at work became increasingly difficult - every time she walked through that lobby, she felt like she was reliving that terrible night. Her colleagues began to notice a change in her - she was withdrawn and preoccupied, always glancing nervously at the stairwell. One day, Manaia's manager called her into his office, concerned about her performance. He gently suggested that maybe it was time for her to take a break from security work, but Manaia knew she couldn't just walk away. She felt like she needed to prove to herself and everyone else that she could still do this job, even if it meant constantly confronting the memories of that terrible night. But it wasn't until she received an email from the elderly man's family - a message thanking her for her kindness and expressing their forgiveness - that Manaia realized just how stuck she had become. They forgave her, but could she ever forgive herself? As she read those words on the screen, something shifted inside of her. She knew she couldn't keep living like this - trapped in a cycle of self-blame and avoidance. Manaia finally made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find some way out of this dark tunnel. She didn't know what to expect or even if it would help, but she was willing to try anything to break free from the grip of that traumatic event. As she sat in the waiting room, clutching her copy of the incident report, Manaia felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, she could learn to remember without reliving the pain.
